# Design Docs & RFCs: Capturing Decisions, Building Alignment ## First Principles: Why Design Documents Matter A **design document (design doc)** is a written proposal for a technical system or change. An **RFC (Request for Comments)** is a formal design doc review process used to build consensus before implementation. **Why they matter:** ``` Without a design doc: - Engineer A starts building feature X - Engineer B discovers they're also building feature X - Manager learns about X only at code review - Infrastructure team says X won't scale at month 3 → Rework: 2–4 weeks of lost effort → Misalignment on requirements → No written decision record With a design doc: - Engineer A writes 3-page proposal for feature X - Gets feedback from B, infrastructure team, PM in 2 days - Decision is written and archived - Implementation aligns with agreed scope → 1 week of saved effort → Clear ownership and decision rationale → Future engineers understand WHY, not just WHAT ``` **Core principle:** > Writing forces clarity. Clarity before code saves weeks later. Design docs serve three purposes: 1. **Alignment:** Stakeholders understand the proposal before work begins. 2. **Decision record:** Why was this chosen over alternatives? (invaluable in 6 months) 3. **Teaching:** New hires read old docs to understand system evolution. --- ## The Problem: Scope Creep and Misalignment You're asked to redesign the payment service. Without a doc: ``` Monday 9 AM: "Redesign payment service" Monday 5 PM: Engineer A starts coding state machine Tuesday 8 AM: PM asks, "Does it support refunds?" Tuesday 2 PM: Infrastructure team warns, "Won't work at scale" Wednesday 10 AM: Architect reviews, "This violates our API contract" Thursday: Rework decision. Back to Monday. ``` **Lost:** 1 week. Unclear scope. No written decision. **With a design doc:** ``` Monday 10 AM: Engineer A writes 4-page design doc - Scope: payment creation, cancellation, refunds - Non-goals: subscription billing, tax calculation - Scalability: 10K requests/sec, <100ms P99 - Alternatives considered: state machine vs event log Monday 4 PM: PM, infrastructure, architect review → PM: "Add dispute resolution in phase 2, not scope" → Infrastructure: "Event log design won't work; try state machine" → Architect: "API contract OK; make sure webhooks are idempotent" Tuesday 10 AM: Design doc updated with feedback Tuesday 11 AM: Implementation begins with full alignment ``` **Won:** 1 week saved. Clear scope. Documented rationale. --- ## Design Doc Structure **Typical template (1–5 pages):** ``` # [System Name] Design Doc ## Problem Statement - What's broken? What's the user pain? - Why now? (metrics, urgency) - Link to issue/ticket ## Goals & Non-Goals Goals: 1. Support refunds within 30 seconds 2. Audit trail for all transactions Non-goals: - Subscription billing (Phase 2) - Real-time revenue reporting (separate system) ## Proposed Solution - High-level architecture (ASCII diagram) - Key components (data model, APIs, services) - How does it work? (step-by-step example) ## Alternatives Considered - Alternative A: [why rejected] - Alternative B: [why rejected] - Chosen: [why it's best] ## Scalability & Trade-offs - Expected load: 10K req/sec - Latency target: P99 < 100 ms - Storage: estimate data volume, retention - Trade-offs: consistency vs availability (explain choice) ## Implementation Plan - Phase 1 (weeks 1–2): data model + API - Phase 2 (weeks 3–4): webhook system - Testing: unit, integration, load tests - Rollout: gradual, with feature flags ## Risks & Mitigation - Risk: Database can't handle 10K req/sec → Mitigation: Load test early, shard if needed - Risk: Schema change is backward-incompatible → Mitigation: Dual-write, validate both paths before cutover ## Open Questions - Should refunds be async (eventual consistency)? - Should we support partial refunds? (awaiting PM) ``` --- ## Real Example: Incident Response Through Design Doc **Scenario:** Your payment system has a bug. Transactions are recorded twice. Your manager asks, "How did this happen?" ``` You: "State machine logic was unclear. No one documented the design." Manager: "OK, redesign it. And write it down." You write design doc: - Problem: unclear state transitions (7 states, 21 transitions) - Root cause: no single source of truth - Solution: Event sourcing (immutable event log) - Trade-off: eventual consistency (max 500ms) - Phases: events + replay + cutover Benefits: 1. Writing the doc, you realize: "Webhook retries could cause double-credit" 2. You catch a bug BEFORE code 3. Team understands why Event Sourcing, not Saga 4. In 6 months, new hire reads it and learns system ``` --- ## Decision-Making Framework: Choosing Design Approach When do you write a design doc? ```mermaid graph TD A["Is this a new system
or major change?"] B["Does it touch
multiple teams?"] C["Is the decision
reversible?"] D["Write a full design doc
1–5 pages"] E["Write a short RFC
1 page, async review"] F["Design in code
PR review is sufficient"] A -->|yes| B A -->|no| C B -->|yes| D B -->|no| C C -->|no, costly| D C -->|yes, cheap| E C -->|small refactor| F style D fill:#c8e6c9 style E fill:#fff9c4 style F fill:#ffcc80 ``` --- ## When to Use / When NOT to Use Design Docs | Scenario | Use Doc? | Example | |----------|----------|---------| | New payment system | YES (1–5 pages) | Redesign refund flow | | Database migration | YES (2–4 pages) | PostgreSQL 12 → 15 | | Optimize cache hit rate | MAYBE (1 page) | Change cache key format | | Fix UI button color | NO | Just update in PR | | Add new feature flag | MAYBE (1 page) | Feature flag for new checkout | | Deprecate old API | YES (2 pages) | Why, timeline, migration path | | Refactor code cleanup | NO | Code review is enough | | Change error budget policy | YES (1–2 pages) | How SLOs affect prioritization | --- ## Story Card: RFC Prevents Post-Launch Crisis **Setup:** Team is building a new orders API. One engineer starts coding, another reviews. **Without RFC:** ``` Friday 5 PM: Engineer A submits PR for new /orders endpoint Returns: [order_id, amount, status] Monday 9 AM: Code review Reviewer: "Looks good. Ship it." Monday 2 PM: Deployed to production Monday 6 PM: Dashboard breaks Root cause: Dashboard expects (amount_usd, timestamp) but gets (amount, status) Solution: Pull PR, rebuild, re-deploy Time lost: 4 hours, customer impact: billing page down ``` **With RFC:** ``` Friday 10 AM: Engineer A writes 2-page RFC for /orders endpoint Proposes: [order_id, amount_usd, timestamp, status] Friday 11 AM: Reviewer (who owns dashboard) sees RFC Feedback: "amount_usd not amount. And add timestamp for sorting." Friday 2 PM: RFC updated and approved Friday 3 PM: Implementation starts with correct schema Monday: Deploy without incident Zero customer impact, correct schema first try. ``` **Key learning:** RFC catches integration issues BEFORE code, when fixing is cheap. --- ## Reasoning Framework: RFC Process ``` Is this a new system or cross-team change? → YES: Write design doc (1–5 pages) → Review with stakeholders (2–5 days) → Iterate based on feedback → Lock decision: "RFC approved" → Code now matches agreed design → NO (single team, small change): Write short RFC (1 page) → 24-hour review → Approve or request changes → Implement → NO (small, reversible change): Design in code → PR review is the design review → This is fine for refactors, minor features ``` --- ## Q&A (Built on Fundamentals) **Recall 1:** You're asked to redesign the payment system. What should you do first? *Must-say:* - Write a design doc or RFC - Identify stakeholders (PM, infrastructure, security) - Define scope, non-goals, alternatives - Get alignment before coding **Probe 1:** Your team has a 3-person frontend feature. Do you need a design doc? *Expected:* - Depends: Is it isolated or does it touch backend/data? - If isolated and reversible: maybe just PR review is enough - If it changes API contract: yes, write 1-page RFC - If it requires new service: yes, 3–5 page doc **Probe 2:** You write a design doc. The architect disagrees with your choice. What now? *Expected:* - This is normal. Don't take it personally. - Understand their concern: scalability? cost? operational burden? - Propose compromise: "What if we use [choice A] for phase 1 and [choice B] for phase 2?" - If still stuck: escalate to decision-maker (who owns the service?) - Document the decision and rationale, even if you disagree **Numeric 1:** Your design doc estimates a system will handle 10K requests/second. Your infrastructure team says the database can only do 5K/sec. What do you change? *Working:* - Option A: Redesign for 5K requests/sec, launch slower - Option B: Add caching to reduce DB load (probabilistic: 5K * 0.3 cache hit rate = 1.5K DB requests) - Option C: Shard the database (10K / 3 shards = 3.3K per shard, under 5K limit) - Best: Option B+C combined. Revisit design doc with new numbers. **Numeric 2:** You're building a new service with 3 teams (frontend, backend, data). How long should RFC review take? How many reviewers? *Working:* - Typical: 2–5 day async review period - Reviewers: architect (1), PM (1), each team lead (3) = 5 people - Decision: RFC approved when architect + at least 2 team leads sign off - Escalation: If blocked after 5 days, discuss synchronously - Document decision in the RFC, even if not unanimous --- ## Questions for the Interviewer - How do you handle disagreement in design reviews? - What's the worst case of "no design doc"? (story time) - How do you decide scope in a design doc? - Have you redesigned something and wished you'd documented the first design? - What's your bar for "this needs a doc" vs "just code it"? --- ## Checklist: Design Doc Quality - [ ] **1. Problem is clear:** Reader understands what's broken and why NOW - ❌ Wrong: "We need a better payment system" - ✓ Right: "Refunds take 3 days; customer support gets 50 complaints/week; we lose $X revenue/month" - [ ] **2. Non-goals are explicit:** What's NOT in scope? - ❌ Wrong: Design doc doesn't mention what's out of scope - ✓ Right: "Phase 1 is refunds only; subscription billing is phase 2, deferred" - [ ] **3. Alternatives are real:** You considered real options and explain tradeoffs - ❌ Wrong: "Alternative A: bad, Alternative B: good" (no reasoning) - ✓ Right: "Alternative A (Saga pattern): simpler but eventual consistency. Alternative B (Event Sourcing): complex but stronger guarantees. We pick B because..." - [ ] **4. Scalability is numbered:** Not vague ("big scale"). Use numbers. - ❌ Wrong: "System must be scalable" - ✓ Right: "10K req/sec P99 latency <100ms; 1 year data retention = 32 TB" - [ ] **5. Open questions are honest:** Flag unknowns - ❌ Wrong: Design doc says everything is locked in day 1 - ✓ Right: "Open question: should refunds be async? Awaiting PM input. Decision blocks phase 2."
